questionStem: A 6-year-o ld boy is brought to the physician by his parents because he continues to wet the bed approx imately five times weekly. He has never had a sustained dry period longer than 7 days. Most of the "accide nts" occur during the first 3 hours of the night and occas ionally during dreams in which he imagines himself urinating. He is afraid to go to friends' houses for sleepovers because of this problem. He worries that his friends would make fun of him if they knew, and he freque ntly feels bad about hims,elf "because I pee the bed like a baby." He was diagnosed with type 1 diabetes mellitus 1 year ago. It is well controlled with insulin, and he is compliant with the medication regimen. Examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's bed-wetting?

choices.E: Urinary overflow incontinence secondary to diabetes mellitus

correctExplanation: Primary enuresis refers to episodic urinary incontinence occurring in children older than 5 years. The episodes commonly lead to adjustment problems and low self-esteem. The pathogenesis of primary enuresis most common ly involves a delay in maturation, though it may alternatively be related to a small functiona l bladder capacity or genetic factors. Along with a voiding diary, patients with nocturnal enuresis should undergo a thorough history, physical examination, and urinalysis to rule out medical causes (eg, bladder dysfunction, urinary tract infection). Many patients with primary enuresis spontaneous ly improve, though motivational therapy (eg, rewarding the patient for urinating prior to bed or having incontinence-free nights) may hasten improvement. In patients with persistent enuresis or enuresis associated with emotional problems, management with enuresis alarms or desmopressin is indicated.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice A) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. This patient's worry is specific to nocturna l urinary incontinence. Oppositional defiant disorder (Choice B) manifests as a persistent pattern of angry mood, defiant behavior, and vindictiveness that causes distress and impaired functioning in the child or their caretakers. This child's enuresis is not a voluntary behavior. Social phobia (Choice D), also known as social anxiety disorder, refers to an excessive fear of scrutiny, embarrassment, or rejection in social or performance situations leading to significant distress or impaired functioning. This patient's anxiety in social situations is secondary to enuresis.

questionStem: A 77-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician by her daughter beca use of a 3-year history of worsening forgetfulness. The patient says that she has not had any problems and does not know why her daughter is so concerned. She is able to recall zero of three objects after 5 minutes . She has significant deficits in praxis, verbal category fluency, and naming . The remainder of the examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference range. Which of the following neurotra nsmitters is most closely associated with the pathophysiology of this patient's illness?
correctExplanation: Dementia, Alzheimer type, results from decreased cholinergic signaling. Cholinergic neurons, which primarily originate from the locus coeruleus and basal forebrain, project widely to areas including the cerebral cortex to mediate attention, learning, and memory. In dementia, Alzheimer type, a proteinopathy involving amyloid and tau proteins leads to the degeneration of cholinergic neurons. Dementia, Alzheimer type, is the most preva lent dementia, presenting with progressive cognitive decline that begins with short-term memory impairment and decline in visuospatia l abilities, and progresses to apraxia, language abnormalities, and dysexecutive syndrome. The disease culminates in behavioral and personality changes that prevent the patient from performing basic activities of daily living such as bathing. Acety lcholinesterase normal ly hydro lyzes acetylcholine in synaptic clefts. Donepezi l and other cholinesterase inhibitors noncompetitively and reversib ly inhibit acetylcholinesterase activity and thereby increase the amount of synaptic acetylcholine available for neurotransmission. Though donepezil may slow the rate of cognitive decline and modest ly improve functionality, donepezil and the other cholinesterase inhibitors are not curative.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. y-Aminobutyric acid (Choice B), GABA, is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter. GABA deficiency is implicated in diseases of central nervous system hyperexcitability but not dementia, Alzheimer type. Dopamine (Choice C) is a monoamine neurotransmitter that mediates reward in the mesolimbic pathway and movement in the basal ganglia. Dopamine excess in the mesolimbic pathway is implicated in psychosis. Dopamine deficiency in the basal ganglia leads to parkinsonism. Dopamine is not known to play a significant role in the pathogenesis of dementia, Alzheimer type.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld man with Parkinson disease is brought to the physician by his wife for a follow-up examination 6 weeks after pramipexole was added to his regimen of carbidopa- levodopa to manage increasingly severe bradykinesia. The patient reports improved movement and greater stability with walking. His wife says that he has become increasingly suspicious of her and has accused her of infidelity. Last week, she awoke during the night and found him sitting in the living room with his hunting rifle on his knees. The patient had insisted that a prowler or "her paramour" was sneaking around the house, and he intended to "teach him a lesson he won't have to learn twice." The patient has no history of psychiatric illness, but his wife says he has seemed depressed and has had decreased appetite and motivation during the past 4 weeks. The patient just shrugs his shoulders in response to his wife's comment. He has hypertens ion control led with lisinopril and hyperlipidemia controlled with lovastatin. His blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. Examination shows less rigidity and increased arm swing compared with examination results 6 weeks ago. On mental status examination, he is coopera tive and superficially polite. He has a mildly dysphoric mood and restricted affect. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's change in mental status?
correctExplanation: Pramipexole increases dopamine concentrations in several brain areas. In the dorsal striatum, an increased dopamine concentration leads to improvement in Parkinson symptoms. In the ventral striatum, dopamine-enhancing medications may lead to mood dysregulation or depression (commonly manifesting with somatic or neurovegetative symptoms). In the limbic system, an increased dopamine concentration leads to psychotic symptoms such as paranoid delusions, hallucinations, and an incongruent affect (as demonstrated by this patient). Distressing psychotic symptoms in the setting of Parkinson disease treatment are typically managed with antipsychotic medication or a decreased dose of the inciting medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Delusional disorder (Choice B) is characterized by the presence of one or more delusions (fixed, false beliefs) for a month or longer without other psychotic symptoms. This patient does not demonstrate one circumscribed delusion, instead presenting with general paranoia (against his wife, her "paramour," a prowler). Further, the onset of psychotic symptoms correlates with the initiation of pramipexole. questionStem: A 25-yea r-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her mother, who reports that the patient has been threatening her at home during the past 2 weeks. The patient has a 5-year history of schizophrenia. Her psychiatric symptoms had been "fairly" well controlled with oral quetiapi ne for 6 months, but she reports that she stopped taking her medication 6 weeks ago because it was sedating her. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Mental status exam ination shows an agitated mood and a guarded affect. She appears to be responding to internal stimuli. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in pharmacothe rapy?

choices.B: Switch from quetiapine to amitripty line

correctExplanation: Schizophrenia is characterized by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms (eg, alogia, apathy, flattened affect). Treatment requires long-term antipsychotic medication. In patients with a partial response to an antipsychotic, a dose increase should be considered. However, intolerable side effects may limit the maximum acceptable dose. Quetiapine is an atypica l antipsychotic medication that primarily antagonizes dopamine-2 receptors and serotonin receptors. Quetiapine also antagonizes histamine receptors, adrenoreceptors, and muscarinic receptors, leading to sedation, weight gain, orthostatic hypotension, and anticholinergic side effects (eg, dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation). This patient experiencing the combination of intolerable sedation (leading to nonadherence) and incomplete control of psychotic symptoms should be trialed on a less sedating antipsychotic medication. Aripiprazo le is an antipsychotic medication with a lower affinity for histamine and acetylcho line receptors and is therefore less likely to cause sedation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Increasing the dosage of quetiapine (Choice A) would likely worsen this patient's sedation. She has already self-discontinued quetiapine because of sedation, so increasing the dosage would make her even less likely to adhere to the medication regimen. Switching from quetiapine to amitriptyline (Choice B) or bupropion (Choice D), antidepressant medications, would not address this patient's psychotic symptoms. This patient should be switched to a different antipsychotic medication. Switching from quetiapine to chlorpromazine (Choice E) would be less likely to resolve the patient's sedation. Chlorpromazine is a low­ potency typical antipsychotic that antagonizes histamine receptors, adrenoreceptors, and muscarinic receptors. It commonly causes sedation.

Acute hyponatremia occurs in 24 to 48 hours and commonly presents with symptoms of nausea, malaise, lethargy, obtundation or coma, and seizures secondary to cerebra l edema, as water is drawn into the neurona l cells in the setting of hypotonic interstitia l fluid. Given the rapid decline in sodium, symptoms can even present with sodium concentrations of 130 mEq/L. In chronic hyponatremia, however, symptoms generally do not present until the hyponatremia has become significant (usually less than 120 mEq/L). Symptoms include fatigue, nausea, forgetfu lness, lethargy, and confusion. Hydrochlorothiazide and other thiazide diuretics can induce hyponatremia because of impaired urine dilution. Since they act on sodium-ch loride symporters in the distal tubule, they do not affect the medullary gradient or the action of antidiuretic hormone. Therefore, these patients can lose sodium in excess of water leading to euvolemic (but also hypovolemic) hyponatremia. The loss of excess solutes in relation to the loss of water also explains this patient's hypokalemia and hypochloremia. Treatment of diuretic-induced hyponatremia involves discontinuing the causative agent, restoring euvolemia if the patient is not euvolemic, and restricting free water intake.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adverse effect of captopril therapy (Choice A) is incorrect. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, such as captopril, are used in the treatment of hypertension, diabetic nephropathy, and congestive heart failure. Adverse effects include cough, hypotension, acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, and angioedema. This patient has hypokalemia, making hydrochlorothiazide-induced hyponatremia the more likely cause of her hyponatremia and altered mental status. Adverse effect of lovastatin therapy (Choice C) is incorrect. Statins are used in the treatment of hyperlipidemia, particularly in patients with clinical signs or symptoms of atherosclerotic cardiovascu lar disease. A common side effect of statins is myopathy, which can present with fatigue and muscle weakness. However, statins do not cause hyponatremia and are unlikely to cause altered mental status. A cerebral infarction (Choice D) is caused by occlusion of a cerebral artery and presents with focal neurologic symptoms, such as hemiparesis or aphasia. It would be unlikely to present solely with mental status changes, particularly in the absence of changes on a CT scan of the head. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice E), presents with impairments in language, memory, perception, motor skills, attention, orientation, problem-solving, and executive function. Lethargy would be uncommon ear ly in the disease, and this patient's electrolyte abnormalities are more likely contributing to her altered mental status than a primary neurologic disease, making an adverse effect of hydrochlorothiazide the most likely cause of her change in menta l status. Educational Objective: Thiazide diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide, can cause clinical ly significant hyponatremia. Chronic hyponatremia can present with lethargy, fatigue, nausea, forgetfulness, and confusion. Treatment includes discontinuing the causative medication and restricting free water intake until sodium concentrations return to normal.

questionStem: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 2, has had episodes of anxiety, bloating, fatigue, irritability, and breast tenderness for the past 2 years. Her symptoms begin about 10 days before menses and cease with the onset of menses. Physical examina tion is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in patient care?

choices.A: Reassura nce and reexam ination in 6 months
choices.B: Instruction to keep a diary of symptoms for the next two menstrual cycles
choices.D: Measureme nt of serum thyrox ine (T 4), thyroid-stimulating hormone , and prolactin concentratio ns

correctExplanation: Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) consists of affective and somatic symptoms occurring in the week before menses. According to the DSM-5, patients must demonstrate at least five symptoms. The symptoms must include at least one mood symptom (affective !ability, marked irritability, depressed mood, or anxiety) and at least one of the following symptoms: anhedonia, concentration difficulties, decreased energy, hypersomnia or insomnia, increased or decreased appetite, a sense of being overwhelmed, and physical symptoms (eg, breast tenderness, muscle or joint pain, sensation of bloating, weight gain). The symptoms must begin to improve within a few days after menses onset and resolve during the week after menses. The diagnosis is established by the patient's prospective documentation of symptoms in relation to at least two menstrual cycles. The pathogenesis is likely related to modulation of neurotransmitters such as serotonin secondary to changes in estrogen and progesterone concentrations. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are indicated in patients with moderate to severe PMDD, whereas patients with mild PMDD may benefit from counseling about stress reduction and lifestyle changes.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Reassurance and reexamination in 6 months (Choice A) would be inappropriate in this patient who is likely to have a PMDD diagnosis and may benefit from active management with medications or stress reduction techniques. Behavior modification therapy (Choice C) emphasizes reinforcement and punishment of certain behaviors. It is commonly utilized in autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. However, this patient is not demonstrating problematic behaviors that require modification. Measurement of serum thyroxine (T 4), thyroid-stimulating hormone, and prolactin concentrations (Choice D) are unnecessary in patients who meet diagnostic criteria for PMDD. Mood changes related to thyroid dysfunction are accompanied by other physical examination signs of thyroid disease (eg, skin and hair changes) and are not typically episodic.

questionStem: A 48-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter 2 hours after she fell at home. Physical exam ination shows ecchymoses over the left hip and left shoulder but is otherwise normal. During evaluation, the daughter pulls the physician aside and explains that her mother has drunk excessively over the past 12 years. She freque ntly consumes several bottles of wine alone at home each day. She also reports that her mother has been forgetting to take cooking pots off the stove. When the physician continues with the evaluation, the patient behaves as if she has never met the physician before now. On cognitive examination, she recalls zero out of three objects after 5 minutes. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's cognitive decline?
correctExplanation: Patients who chronically abuse alcohol typically demonstrate a significant thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency caused by poor nutritional intake, thiamine malabsorption, and impaired cellular utilization of thiamine. Over time, thiamine deficiency can result in damage and atrophy of the mammillary bodies, visible on MRI of the brain, which manifests as Wernicke encephalopathy. The typical clinical presentation of Wernicke encephalopathy is a triad of acute altered mental status, ophthalmoplegia/nystagmus, and ataxia. The symptoms of Wernicke encephalopathy are reversible but incre,ase the risk for developing Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (also known as Korsakoff psychosis) in chronic alcohol users if not immediately treated with high-dose thiamine. Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome is an irreversible condition that features anterograde and retrograde amnesia along with the consequent tendency to confabulate, or verbalize false stories or memories, to compensate for the inability to remember. This patient demonstrates an inability to form new memories after the amnesia-causing event (anterograde amnesia).
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Choice A) is a human prion disease that presents with rapidly progressing dementia, neuropsychiatric symptoms, cerebellar dysfunction, corticospinal tract dysfunction, basal ganglia dysfunction, and stimulus-induced myoclonus. This patient does not demonstrate stimulus-induced myoclonus or cerebellar, corticospina l, or basal ganglia dysfunction. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice B), is the most prevalent dementia, presenting with progressive cognitive decline that begins with short-term memory impairment, progresses to apraxia and language abnormalities, and culminates in behavioral and personality changes preventing the patient from performing basic activities of daily living. Anterograde memory impairment is common, but this patient's young age is inconsistent with dementia, Alzheimer type.

questionStem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her father as a new patient for a well-child examination. On entering the physician's office, the patient immediately climbs onto the physician's lap and begins talking with the physician. Her father says that his daughter has shown poor learning ability and has outbursts in school. He also says she is highly sensitive to sound. Examination shows a small, upturned nose, small chin, and long philtrum. Muscle tone is decreased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Williams syndrome results from a sporadic or inherited deletion of contiguous genes on chromosome 7q11.23, including the elastin gene. Patients typically present with an overly friendly demeanor, emotiona l dysregulation, intellectual delay, elfin facies (strabismus, flat nasal bridge, short nose, long philtrum, wide mouth), short stature, vascular and cardiac valve abnormalities seconda ry to elastin dysfunction, structura l abnormalities of the urinary tract, and endocrine abnormalities (eg, hypothyroidism). Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing confirming a deletion on chromosome 7q 11.23. !Management involves surgica l correction of vascula r, cardiac, or other functionally significant structu ral abnormalities and antihypertensive medication if such develops.

It is characterized by growth delay, intellectual disability, facial dysmorphia (microcephaly, arched eyebrows, small upturned nose, widely spaced teeth), and malformations of the extremities. Down syndrome (Choice B) results from trisomy of chromosome 21 and presents with characteristic physical features including broad, flat, facial features with prominent epicanthal folds and a single palmar crease. Patients with Down syndrome also present with cognitive impairment, cardiac abnormalities (eg, atrial septal defect), gastrointestinal abnormalities (eg, duodenal atresia, imperforate anus), ophthalmologic abnormalities (eg, refractive errors), and hearing loss. questionStem: A 77-year-o ld woman comes to the physician at the request of an attorney prior to writing an advance directive. She says that she wants to have an advance directive in order to avoid putting an unnecessa ry burden on her children. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. She immigrated to the USA from Poland 20 years ago. She has only an elementary school education. She was employed in a cleaning service for a hotel but stopped working 5 years ago. She lives alone and is able to perform activities of daily living independently. She participates in social activities at her church. All of her close friends are also from Poland. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. On mental status exam ination, she is nervous . She is alert and is oriented to person. She knows she is in the physician's office but does not recall the street name correctly. She knows the month and day of the week but is not sure of the exact date. She knows her address. She can recall two of three words after 5 minutes. She can subtract 7 from 100 using her fingers but is unable to subtract 7 from 93. She is unable to spell the word "world" backwards. She can draw the hands on a clock to show 10 minutes to 2 o'clock and can slowly copy a drawing of two intersecting pentagons. She demonstrates that she understands the meaning of a standardized story. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step with respect to this patient's advance directive?

choices.A: Discussion of her preferences for care
choices.C: Repeat her mental status examinat ion with an interprete

correctExplanation: Though some cognitively impaired patients may lack capacity to make decisions about their care, cognitive ly impaired patients should not be assumed to lack decisional capacity. Though this patient illustrates mild abnormalities on brief cognitive testing (which may indicate normal aging changes in a patient with a limited education), these findings do not necessarily preclude her from making end-of­ life decisions. To meet the criteria for decisional capacity, patients must express a consisten t choice, demonstrate an understanding of the risks and benefits of the choice, demonstrate an appreciation of the significance of the choice for their personal circumstances, and illustrate an ability to reason through the options. Therefore, to assess this patient's decisional capacity and potentially write her advance directive (if the physician believes the patient possesses decisional capacity), the physician should discuss the patient's preferences for care and assess the four decisional capacity criteria specific to these decisions.

A fluctuating cognitive course (eg, delirium) is unlikely in this patient with mild cognitive impairment who is consistently alert, attentive (difficulty with serial ?sand spelling "world" is likely secondary to this patient's limited education given her ability to attend to and understand a story), and able to verbalize a desire to write an advance directive.

correctExplanation: Headaches can be differentiated into primary and secondary headaches (eg, substances, infection, neoplasm, trauma). Headache features that raise concern for serious secondary causes include fever, focal neurologic deficits, abrupt onset, history of malignancy or trauma , and positional exacerbation. Caffeine withdrawal typically presents with headache, fatigue, depressed or irritable mood, difficu lty concentrating, gastrointestinal distress, tachycardia, hand tremor, or flu-like symptoms. The headache is common ly diffuse and pulsating, varies from mild to severe in intensity, begins within 24 hours of last caffeine consump tion , and improves once withdrawal resolves. Acute management may include over-the-counter analgesics or the administration of caffeine. Patients desiring to abstain from caffeine should gradually taper their use to prevent severe withdrawal symptoms.

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 1-year history of difficulty sitting still for more than 1 hour. He says that he has a nearly intolerable sensation of restlessness in his legs when watching movies or during long flights. His symptoms resolve when he stands up and takes a few steps. He also has had difficulty falling asleep because of his symptoms and states that he thinks he moves around a lot once he falls asleep because his wife often complains that he kicks her in bed. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Deep tendon reflexes are normal in all extremities. Sensation is intact. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial pharmacothe rapy?
correctExplanation: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common movement disorder characterized by an urge to move the lower extremities when sitting or lying down to sleep. During sleep, many patients with RLS demonstrate periodic movements of the lower extremities. The pathogenesis is incomplete ly understood, but alterations in dopamine metabolism and cellular iron influx and efflux may be involved. Caffeine along with antihistamine, dopamine antagonist, and antidepressant medications common ly exacerbate RLS. All patients with RLS should undergo iron studies. Patients with iron deficiency require iron repletion. In patients without iron deficiency who report chronic and severe symptoms, dopamine agonists such as ropinirole are indicated.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hydroxyzine (Choice A) is an antihistamine medication utilized for allergic reactions and off-label for anxiety. It common ly exacerbates RLS. Modafinil (Choice B) is commonly utilized to address daytime sleepiness in patients with narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea, and shift­ work sleep disorder. It has no proven efficacy in RLS. Trazodone (Choice D) is a serotonin modulator, and zolpidem (Choice E) is a nonbenzodiazepine sedative-hypnotic medication. Both are utilized to treat insomnia but are not helpful in RLS. Educational Objective: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) is a common movement disorder characterized by an urge to move the lower extremities when lying down to sleep. During sleep, many patients with RLS demonstrate periodic movements of the lower extremities. . - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - .

questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because her husband is concerned that she has been having difficulty remembe ring things around the house. During the past 6 weeks, she has been forgetting to do her usual household chores. She does not think that she has a problem. She says that she does her best but often feels fatigued, especial ly when moving around a lot. She has had numbness of both legs and intermittent blurred vision during the past year. Physical examination shows pallor of the optic discs. Deep tendon reflexes at the knees and ankles are brisk bilatera lly. On mental status examination, she has an upbeat mood and affect. She is oriented to person, place, and time. She has difficulty remem bering the names of recent U.S. Presidents. There is no evidence of auditory or visual hallucinations. A T2-weighted MRI of the brain shows numerous small plaques in the periventricular white matter. A lumbar puncture is done. Which of the following findings is most likely on cerebrospina l fluid analysis?
correctExplanation: Multiple sclerosis, the most prevalent immune-mediated demyelinating disease, can present initially with lesions in several central nervous system (CNS) locations. According to the McDonald criteria for multiple sclerosis diagnosis, patients must have evidence of demyelinating lesions that are separated in time and location. This evidence can be based on subjective symptoms or imaging evidence. This patient demonstrated several episodes of optic neuritis separated in time, along with dysfunction of the dorsal column­ medial lemniscus tracts (decreased sensation), corticospinal tracts (hyperreflexia), frontal lobes (incongruent ly bright affect), and medial temporal lobe (decreased recall memory), representing separation in space. Fatigue and symptom exacerbation with exercise are common in multiple sclerosis. MRI of the brain typically shows focal white matter hyperintensities in the periventricular region, cortex, subcortical region, cerebellum, or spine. Oligoclonal bands of immunoglobulins, indicating immune overactivation, can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid but are not necessary for diagnosis. Treatment includes corticosteroids for symptomatic management of acute flares and long-term disease-modifying treatments such as interferon or monoclonal antibodies, which decrease the frequency of future episodes.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Decreased glucose (Choice A) is demonstrated in bacterial and fungal meningitis or encephalitis. Eosinophilocytosis (Choice C) is consisten t with eosinophilic meningitis secondary to parasitic infections. This patient's focal neurologic deficits and chronic course along with the absence of headache, encephalopathy (eg, decreased alertness, disorientation), or systemic signs of infection are more consisten t with multiple sclerosis.

questionStem: A 57-year-o ld lawyer is brought to the emergency department by police after he interrupted a church service by loudly proclaim ing that he is the Messiah. Police say that he became angry and physically confronta tional when he was asked to leave and continued to insist that he was the Messiah when police intervened . On arrival in the emergency department, he is expansive and talks loudly. He appears well groomed. On questioning, he says he has never been sick and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He refuses to allow a physical examination and becomes irritable with the nurses. He dema nds to see the person in charge of the hospital, noting he has figured out a way to save the hospital millions of dollars. Acute mania typically manifests with an expansive or euphoric or irritable mood, increased energy, a decreased need for sleep, increased goal-directed activity, rapid speech and thinking (as evidenced by this patient's pressured speech with a flight of ideas), irresponsibility (as evidenced by this patient's disruption of a church service), and grandiose thinking (as evidenced by this patient's confidence that his plan can save the hospital millions of dollars). The increased norepinephrine causes tachycardia and hypertension through activation of sympathetic adrenoceptors, leading to increased cardiac chronot ropy and peripheral vasoconstriction. questionStem: A 37-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of recurrent thoughts that she has sexually abused her 5-year-old daughter. She says that she examines her daughter's perineum several times daily looking for evidence of abuse. Examination of the child by her pediatrician has shown no evidence of abuse. The patient believes that she is going crazy. She reports that she was sexually abused as a child. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, she appears tense, anxious, and mildly depressed. She cries as she describes her worrisome thoughts. There is no evidence of hallucinations . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is an anxiety disorder typica lly characterized by obsessions that the patient attempts to neutralize with compu lsions. Obsessions are unwanted, intrusive thoughts (eg, thoughts related to violence, sex, or contamination) or urges (eg, to commit violence) that increase anxiety. Compulsions are rigidly applied repetitive behaviors (eg, checking, washing) or mental activities (eg, counting, repeating words) that relieve anxiety related to obsessions. By definition, the compulsions are excessive or do not realistica lly address the obsessive fears, and patients commonly recognize the irrationality of their compulsions. The pathogenesis of OCD is likely multifactorial, related to genetics, stress, or dysfunction of striatal and thalamic circuits. Treatment includes high doses of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRls, eg, fluoxetine) or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with a focus on exposure to the discomfort of suppressing the compulsion after experiencing the obsession.

Acute stress disorder (Choice A) refers to intrusive thoughts, hyperarousal, avoidance, or negative mood and thoughts that occur within 1 month of a traumatic event such as a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. This patient has no history of a traumatic event within the past month. Delusional disorder (Choice B) is characterized by the presence of one or more delusions for a month or longer without other psychotic symptoms. Patients typically lack insight into their delusion, which they accept as truth. As such, delusiona l thoughts are usually ego­ syntonic and nondistressing. questionStem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination. correctExplanation: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) presents with chronic symptoms of hyperactivity/impulsivity or inattention that occur in more than one setting and impair academic, social, or emotional function. Children with predominant hyperactivity symptoms are unable to sit still and may have difficulty taking turns (postulated to result from a dysregulated dopamine reward pathway), whereas children with predominant inattentive symptoms tend to daydream, process information slowly, and demonstrate difficulty in completing tasks (related to norepinephrine dysregulation). ADHD is associated with soft neurologic abnorma lities such as brief reflexes. For diagnosis, physicians must establish that the patient is functional ly impaired in severa l settings, so parents and teachers must fill out behavioral rating scales. Stimulants, which include amphetamine salts and methylphenidate, are first-line agents for treatment that increase synaptic dopamine and norepinephrine.

questionStem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department by paramedics 30 minutes after his friends noticed that he had become confused and unsteady . His friends reported tha t he "may have been trying to get high." Glucose and naloxone administered en route to the emergency department produced no change in his condition. On arrival, he is lethargic , and his speech is slurred. His temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg. His gait is ataxic. The patient falls asleep for 1 hour, and a second neurologic examination on awakening shows full alertness and a normal gait. Which of the following substances is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Inhalant abuse (eg, toluene, nitrous oxide, spray paint, glue) is common in children and adolescents. The effects typica lly begin within seconds of use and persist for approximately 30 minutes, representing a faster onset and resolution compared with other recreationa l drugs. Inhalants exert effects on multiple organ systems: dermato logic (eg, perioral or perinasal dermatitis with erythro- or pyoderma), otolaryngologic (eg, nosebleeds, halitosis), ocular (eg, conjunctiva! infection), cardiac (eg, dysrhythmia, tachycardia), gastrointestinal (eg, nausea, anorexia), respiratory (eg, wheezing, coughing, sneezing), and neuropsychiatric (eg, headache, ataxia, anosmia, slurred speech, mood swings, hallucinations). Severe inhalant toxicity can manifest with tachydysrhythmias and respiratory depression, and ultimate ly seizures or coma. Treatment is primari ly supportive, though some inhalants have specific antidotes (eg, methylene blue for nitrites). Prevention is key; schoo ls shou ld monitor the use of solvent-based products, and parents and children should be educated about the risks of inhalants.

However, alcohol is typically metabolized over the course of hours, not minutes. Cocaine (Choice B) is a CNS stimulant that causes euphoria and increases sympathetic tone, leading to tachycardia and hypertension, pupillary dilation, and restlessness (rather than lethargy). Also, cocaine is typical ly metabo lized over hours, not minutes. Heroin (Choice C) causes symptoms of CNS depression including sedation, respiratory depression, bradycardia, and hypotension. However, heroin is typical ly metabo lized over the course of hours, not minutes. Also, if the patient were intoxicated with opioids, his lethargy would be expected to rapidly improve with naloxone therapy.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 57-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of memory loss for 3 months. Examination shows a very sluggish patient with a flat affect who talks slowly and in a whisper. Initially, she replies to all mental status tests, "I don't know" or "I can't remem ber." As the physician shows a warm and supportive manner, her responses improve, so that eventual ly she recalls the main event in the news the previous evening and is able to recall two out of three objects after 5 minutes. She is told the third object. When retested just before leaving 10 minutes later, she recalls all three. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?

correctExplanation: Symptoms of major depressive disorder (MOD) include 2 or more weeks of at least five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, psychomotor retardation, suicidal thoughts, or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). This patient's subjective memory loss and severe psychomotor retardation that improve as she develops a rapport with the physician likely represents a functional neurologic disorder (reflecting the conversion of emotional distress into neurologic symptoms), which is frequently comorbid with depression. questionStem: A 21-year-o ld college student is brought to the emergency department by her roommates because of a 4-day history of progressive general ized weakness and muscle cramps. correctExplanation: Bulimia nervosa (binging/purging type) involves cycles of uncontrollable eating and compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, laxative, or diuretic overuse that occur at least once a week for 3 months or more. Treatment of bulimia nervosa is through a combined medical and psychiatric approach, and it involves correcting fluid and electrolyte derangements alongside behavioral and pharmacologic therapy.

questionStem: A 23-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by police after he had to be removed in handcuffs from an airliner on which he had been a passenger. The airline attendants report that the patient shouted that he was a pilot and demanded to fly the plane, because he was too busy to wait for "those idiots that the airline calls pilots to take off." The patient reports, "I felt exquis ite and perfectly glorious until those Keystone Cops started harassing me." A court-ordered evaluat ion shows the stealing to be the latest in a series of self-defeating behaviors over the past 2 months that include incomplete homewor k assignments and truancy. He states that he has difficulty concentrating and awake ns frequentlly at night. During an interview with his family, the teenage r seems oblivious to the obvious marital discord between his parents. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

The emotiona l disturbance manifests as marked distress out of proportion to the stressor and a significant impairment in daily school, work, or social functioning. Patients may internalize or externalize their distress, resulting in depression or anxiety symptoms or conduct disturbances (acting out), respectively. Patients with adjustment disorder do not meet criteria of anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. This patient has some anxiety/depression symptoms (eg, difficulty concentrating and sleeping) and conduct disturbances (eg, truancy) with a clear stressor and without meeting the criteria for anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. Treatment includes high doses of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRls) or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), also referred to as behavior therapy, with a focus on exposure to the discomfort of suppressing the compulsion after experiencing the obsession. In patients who opt to try medication first and experience a partial response, physicians may augment with an antipsychotic medication (eg, risperidone) or CBT.

questionStem: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents for a physical examination prior to participating in school sports. Her parents are concerned about her academ ic performance because she has received mostly B's and C's. Her parents and older brother attended Ivy League colleges. Every time they try to discuss applying to colleges, she becomes angry and tearful and goes to her room, slamming the door and refusing to talk about it. They try to talk to her through the closed door, but she will not cooperate. They have arranged alumn i interviews for her at their own alma maters, and they are concerned that this negative attitude will impact her interviews. When they contacted her guidance counselor about their concerns and observations, he was surprised and reported that she has been diligently working on her applications with his help. She is at the 50th percentile for height and 30th percent ile for weight. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examinat ion, she is cooperative but reticent. Her speech is articulate and coherent. Wh ich of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: Parental expectations exert a strong influence on children's wel l-being. Unrealistically high expectations common ly lead to the child feeling disappointed and inadequate. These feelings may be internalized (eg, lead to depression) or externalized (eg, acting out, such as slamming the door). This patient's emotional dysregulation and uncooperative behavior when her parents communicate or imply high expectations about her academic performance is an age-appropriate reaction. Parents should critical ly examine whether their expectations are realistic and communicate acceptance to their child to avoid these emotiona l difficulties.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Adjustment disorder with anxious mood (Choice A) or depressed mood (Choice B) refers to the onset of disproportionate distress manifested as anxiety or depression symptoms, respectively, within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. This patient does not demonstrate anxiety or depression symptoms. As well, her uncooperative behaviors are specific to situations when her parents communicate their high expectations, whereas patients with adjustment disorder demonstrate consistent depression, anxiety, or conduct disturbances. Dysthymic disorder (Choice C), more common ly known as persistent depressive disorder, refers to depression symptoms lasting longer than 2 years. This patient does not endorse depressive symptoms and has not illustrated behavior changes for more than 2 years.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld man who is a resident of a skilled nursing care facility is brought to the emergency department because of sweating and increas ing confusion for 2 days. He underwent a below-the-k nee amputat ion 4 weeks ago for osteomyelitis. He has a 15-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with glybur ide. He also is receiving acetaminophen and codeine for pain, allopurino l for gout, and haloperido l for nighttime agitation. His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1 °F), pulse is 120/min, and blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg. Muscle tone is increased. The patient is too disoriented to respond appropriate ly to questions. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit Leukocyte count Serum Na+ Glucose 50% 8000/mm 3 with a normal differentia l 154 mEq/L 175 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
correctExplanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient who has received high-potency antipsychotic medication (haloperidol). NMS is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction (eg, tachycardia, sweating). Common causative agents are antipsychotics (especia lly high-potency antipsychotics) and antidopaminergic nausea medications. Rigidity results from dopamine antagonism in the nigrostriatal pathway, while autonomic dysfunction and hyperthermia may result from dopamine antagonism in the hypothalamus. Characteristic laboratory abnorma lities include leukocytosis and increased serum creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and alkaline phosphatase concentrations (caused by prolonged muscle rigidity and consequent myocyte damage). Electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hypo- or hypernatremia, hypocalcemia) may also be demonstrated. Treatment is supportive and includes discontinuation of the offending medication, hydration, cooling blankets, and benzodiazepines, if needed, for agitation.

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld woman comes to the physician to request a sedative to help calm her nerves. She has had extreme anxiety and difficulty eating and sleeping since she received the diagnosis of breast cancer 10 days ago. She is married and has two children, and she worries constantly about what will happen to them if she dies. She regularly volunteers at the school library, but she has been unable to go because of her anxiety since her diagnosis. She has not felt depressed, guilty, or suicidal. She has no other history of serious medical or psychiatric illness. There is no family history of psychiatric illness. Physical examination shows a healing incision over the breast biopsy site. On mental status examination, she is anxious but shows a full range of affect. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Adjustment disorder refers to the onset of an emotional disturbance within 3 months of an identifiable stressor. The emotional disturbance manifests as marked distress out of proportion to the stresso r and a significant impairment in daily school, work, or social functioning. Patients may internalize or externalize their distress, resulting in depression and anxiety symptoms or conduct disturbances, respectively. Patients with adjustment disorder do not meet criteria of anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. This patient has some anxiety and depression symptoms (anxiety, insomnia, decreased appetite) with a clear stresso r and without meeting the criteria for anxiety, depressive, or conduct disorders. As adjustment disorder is typically self-limited, the treatment of adjustment disorder commonly includes brief supportive psychotherapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Acute stress disorder (Choice A) refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts or memories, changes in arousal and reactivity (eg, hypervigilance ), avoidance of reminders of trauma, and negative mood/thoughts that occur within 1 month of a traumatic event such as physical or sexual violence. This patient has not experienced a violent event and is not reporting intrusive thoughts, avoidance of reminders of her stressor (she is instead constant ly worrying about the stressor), or a depressed mood. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice C) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. This patient's anxiety is specific to her new diagnosis. • I I• I • • I I I• I• I • • I I I I • •II • • I

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician by her family 1 week after the sudden onset of bizarre behavior that began after she had a disagreement with her supervisor at work. The supervisor told her fam ily that she became confused and began to accuse him of monitoring her phone calls and watching her every move because he wanted to fire her. Her work performance had been fine. She told her husband that she heard the voices of her coworkers talking about her when she was driving home from work 2 days ago. She used cocaine briefly 5 years ago. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, she is oriented to person and place but not to date. She is unsure why she is being evaluated, and her answers to questions are incomprehensib le at times. She admits to being worried and depressed about her coworkers being "after her." Laboratory studies are within normal limits, and toxicology screening shows traces of marijuana. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Brief psychotic disorder is characterized by the acute onset of one or more psychotic symptoms (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior) lasting less than 1 month. This patient is experiencing a paranoid delusion, disorganized speech, and auditory hallucinations. Risk factors for brief psychotic disorder include stressful life events and personality disorders. Treatment may include hospitalization and antipsychotic treatment depending on symptom severity and functional impairment, though some symptoms or the entire presentation may resolve without medications.

The onset of this patient's psychotic symptoms years after cocaine use is inconsistent with cocaine-induced psychotic disorder. questionStem: A 3-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents because of behavior problems since starting preschool 3 months ago. Her parents report that she was adopted at 2 weeks of age and little is known about her biologic parents. Her teachers report that she is more active than her peers, is easily frustrated, and has frequent tantrums. She is not yet toilet trained. She is at the 20th percentile for height and weight. Physical examination shows a thin upper lip, a narrow philtrum, and bilateral palmar creases. Her gait is normal. On mental status examination, she speaks clearly, communicating in two- to three-word phrases. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Alcohol is a proven teratogen, since alcohol use during pregnancy leads to irreversible fetal neurologic effects and physical malformations in a cluster of symptoms called fetal alcohol syndrome. Fetal alcohol syndrome is a leading cause of intellectual disability in the United States and would explain this patient's behaviora l problems. Because of the failure of cell migration, fetal alcohol syndrome also presents with physica l abnormalities such as microcephaly, facial abnormalities (small palpebral fissures, thin vermi lion border, cleft lip and palate, smooth or long philtrum), limb deformities, and congenital heart disease. Patients with fetal alcoho l syndrome may demonstrate abnormal bone development (eg, cervical spine fusion) and delayed bone growth. Though alcohol is associated with obstetric complications such as preterm birth that commonly result from the use of substances during pregnancy, the physical malformations including those seen in this case are specific to alcohol use.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) (Choice A) is defined as a pattern of inattention or hyperactivity that persists in at least two settings. Patients may demonstrate symptoms of inattention, such as difficulty following instructions, difficulty completing tasks, or a poor attention span in school. Interrupting others, fidgeting, and not waiting one's turn may be symptoms of hyperactivity. This patient's behavioral problems are only seen at school and her unique physical characteristics are not seen in ADHD. Characteristic physical findings of Down syndrome (Choice B) include intellectua l disability, broad, flat, facial features with prominent epicanthal folds, and a single palmar crease. There are similarities between the abnormal facies of patients with fetal alcohol syndrome and Down syndrome, but this patient's combination of growth retardation and characteristic physica l features are most suggestive of fetal alcohol syndrome.

questionStem: A 22-yea r-old college student comes to the physician because of depressed mood, restlessness, irritability, and an inability to concentrate since being raped 1 week ago. She has had difficulty sleeping because of recurrent nightmares about the rape and has not been able to study or attend classes . At times, she feels like the world around her is not real. Physical examination shows no abnormal ities. On mental status examination, she is anxious and tense. She is unable to remembe r the details of the rape and becomes distressed and does not want to talk about it. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Acute stress disorder refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts or memories, changes in arousal and reactivity, avoidance of reminders of trauma, and negative changes in mood or thoughts that occur within 1 month of a traumatic event. The inciting traumatic event is defined as a serious physically or sexually violent experience. Intrusive memories may manifest as daytime flashbacks, nightmares, or dissociative experiences (eg, derealization as in this patient). Changes in arousal and reactivity may manifest as hypervigilance, easy startle, anxiety, restlessness, or decreased concentration. This patient's selective amnesia represents a negative alteration in cognition. Treatment common ly includes trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy rather than medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Brief psychotic disorder (Choice B) is characterized by at least one acute psychotic symptom (eg, delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior) lasting less than 1 month. This patient's belief that the world around her is not real is stress-related rather than rigid, signifying that the belief represents derealization rather than a delusion. Generalized anxiety disorder (Choice C) is an anxiety disorder that features excessive worrying about a range of topics with associated functional impairment. This patient's anxiety is specific to the rape. Major depressive disorder (Choice D) includes 2 or more weeks of five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt or worthlessness, difficulty concentrating, psychomotor retardation, suicidal thoughts, or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). This patient does not meet the symptom or duration criteria for major depressive disorder. Post-traumatic stress disorder (Choice E) refers to symptoms of intrusive thoughts and memories of trauma, hyperarousal, avoidance

questionStem: A 52-year-o ld man with cancer of the tongue comes to the physician 2 days after an episode of anxiety and panic while being fitted with a mask in preparation for radiation therapy. He reports similar symptoms during MRI of the brain; he says he was unable to tolerate being confined to such a small space and felt panic and the need to escape. On physical exam ination, the tongue is enlarged and tender. On mental status examination, he is anxious when descr ibing being confined. The most appropriate pharmacotherapy for this patient targets which of the following neurotransm itters?
correctExplanation: Specific phobia is a psychiatric disorder featuring anxiety about a certain situation or object that leads to avoidance behavior. Common phobias include flying, anima ls, and enclosed spaces. To meet diagnostic criteria, the anxiety symptoms must be persistent (lasting longer than 6 months), and patients must demonstrate significant distress or socia l and occupational impairment. Long-term cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the most effective treatment, though short-term benzodiazepines may be utilized in certain patients whose feared situations occur infrequently (or patients without access to CBT). Benzodiazepines are positive allosteric modulators of the ionotropic y-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAA) receptor, permitting the increased influx of chloride ions and decreased neuronal excitability in brain regions responsib le for fear such as the amygdala.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Medications that increase acety lcholine (Choice A) signaling (eg, cholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezi l) are utilized in dementia and myasthenia gravis. Acety lcholine antagonists (eg, benztropine) lead to relief of drug-induced parkinsonism along with sedation, urinary retention, and constipation. These medications are not utilized to treat acute anxiety. Dopamine (Choice C) agonists (eg, pramipexo le) are utilized for symptomatic treatment in Parkinson disease, while dopamine antagonists (eg, antipsychotic medications) are utilized to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. These medications are less effective than benzodiazepines in treating acute anxiety. Norepinephrine antagonists (Choice D) (eg, ~-adrenergic block,ers such as proprano lol) are common ly utilized for performance anxiety but not specific phobia. Norepinephrine agonists (eg, stimulant medications, clonidine) are commonly used to treat attention­ deficit/hyperactivity disorder. questionStem: A 47-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of decreased libido over the past 2 years. He describes his marriage as good. He is able to achieve erection only through masturbation. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol. He uses marijuana daily. His pulse is 72/min, respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 120/90 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Serum studies show a thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration of 1 µU/ml, thyroxine (T 4) concentration of 7 µg/dl, and triiodothyronine (T 3) concentration of 125 ng/dl. Urine toxicology screening is positive for marijuana. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cannabis use has been associated with erectile dysfunction. The pathogenesis is believed to involve both peripheral vascular endothelial dysfunction and dysregulated endocannabinoid signaling in the hypotha lamus. Testicular atrophy and decreased libido related to cannabis use have been found in animal studies, though human studies of the relationship of cannabis and libido have demonstrated mixed results. Erectile function may be sufficient to allow for nocturnal erections and erections from direct penile stimulation but insufficient to permit the level of rigidity required for penetration. Management of erectile dysfunction requires addressing the underlying cause. To assist in determining the underlying cause and potentia lly addressing the problem, patients with erectile dysfunction who use cannabis should be advised to discontinue cannabis use.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Individual psychotherapy (Choice B) and marital therapy (Choice C) assist in addressing psychogenic causes of erectile dysfunction, which typically present with intact nocturnal and masturbation-induced erections. Marital therapy is unlikely to be helpful given the good relationship between the patient and his partner. This patient should first attempt discontinuing cannabis; if discontinuing cannabis does not lead to improved sexual function, then individual psychotherapy should be considered to address potentia l performance anxiety or another psycho logical cause. Levothyroxine therapy (Choice D) treats sexual dysfunction secondary to hypothyroidism. This patient demonstrates normal thyroid function tests. Sildenafi l therapy (Choice E) promotes vasodilation in the arteries of the corpora cavernosa. In patients with erectile dysfunction secondary to psycho logical causes or substance use, these underlying problems should be addressed first.

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman comes to the physician because she is anxious and concerned that she is contaminating her hands with HIV whenever she touches a door handle. She realizes that this is irrational but nevert heless has to wash her hands repeatedly with household bleach. She estimates that she washes her hands 10 times daily for 10 minutes at a time. Exam ination shows cracked and bleeding hands . Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is an anxiety disorder typica lly characterized by obsessions (unwanted, intrusive thoughts that produce anxiety) that the patient attempts to neutralize with compulsions (repetitive behaviors). By definition, the compulsions are excessive or do not realistica lly address the obsessive fears, and patients commonly recognize the irrationality of their compulsions. This patient's worry about contamination represents an obsession, while her repeated hand washing represents a compulsion. Treatment includes high doses of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRls, eg, fluoxetine) or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with a focus on exposure to the discomfort of suppressing the compulsion after experiencing the obsession. SSRls have the lowest side effect burden of antidepressant medications. Clomipramine (a tricyclic antidepressant) and venlafaxine (a selective serotonin­ norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor antidepressant) are effective second- line agents.

It common ly causes increased anxiety as a side effect and is not a first-line medication for OCD. Buspirone (Choice B) is a serotonin modu lator utilized to treat generalized anxiety disorder. It has no proven efficacy in OCD. Haloperido l (Choice D) is a typica l antipsychotic medication utilized to treat schizophrenia. questionStem: Immediately after undergo ing operative repair of a right knee dislocation, a 42-year-o ld woman has severe pain. She has a history of heroin addiction and has been receiving therapy through a comm unity-based methadone maintenance program . Her methadone maintenance dose has remained constant for 2 years. She has no other history of medical or psychiatric illness. On examinat ion, she rates her pain as a 10 on a 10-point scale, a level that is consistent with that reported by other patients who have undergone this operative procedure. Admin istration of which of the following is most appropriate at this time?

choices.A: A decreased methadone dose and additiona l analges ia on a set schedule
choices.B: A decreased methadone dose and patient-control led analgesia
choices.C: An increased methadone dose and additiona l analgesia on a set schedule
choices.D: The patient's usual methadone maintenance dose and patient-controlled analgesia
choices.E: The patient's usual methadone maintenance dose only

correctExplanation: Methadone is an opioid receptor agonist with a long half-life. While it can be used to treat acute pain, it is often used to treat patients with opioid use disorder. While methadone is common ly dosed once daily when used to treat opioid use disorder, it only provides analgesia for 6 to 8 hours. Therefore, it is not solely efficient for the management of postoperative pain. Current recommendations for acute pain management in patients on methadone maintenance therapy include continuing the baseline methadone dose and supplementing pain control with other non-opioid and opioid agents as needed. Pain control may be more difficult in patients on chronic methadone therapy, as they common ly have cross-to lerance to other opioids. Therefore, continuing this patient's baseline methadone dose and adding a regimen of patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) would be appropriate to allow for sufficient pain relief. As her acute pain declines, the PCA can be weaned.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. A decreased methadone dose and additiona l analgesia on a set schedule (Choice A) would not effectively treat this patient's pain. A decreased dose of methadone would likely exacerbate her pain, and a set schedule of pain medication would not be adequate or flexible enough to control her pain. A decreased methadone dose and patient-controlled analgesia (Choice B) may control this patient's pain but would likely cause her to use an increased amount of intravenous opioids as compared with a regimen with her baseline dose of methadone. An increased methadone dose and additional analgesia on a set schedule (Choice C) may control this patient's pain but would complicate weaning of her medication regimen back to her baseline methadone dose. Additional ly, this patient has been on a stable dose of methadone and adjusting her dose may interfere with her substance use disorder treatment.

questionStem: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of a 3-month history of social withdrawa l and subtle but increasingly odd interpersonal interactions, such as blinking to avoid direct eye contact. He also has a 1-month history of intermittent daydreaming and episodes of talking to himself. His behavior was first noticed by his teacher and the school nurse, who notified his parents. The patient says that when in quiet locations, he hears vague, distorted sounds. He talks to himself to calm himself and to make the sounds disappear. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. His maternal uncle has bipolar disorder, and two paternal uncles have schizophrenia. The patient does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he is alert and fully oriented; he appears shy and has a flat affect. He says his mood is "okay." Further testing is most likely to show which of the following results in this patient?

choices.E: Hyperphospho rylation of the Tau protein

correctExplanation: According to the DSM-5, patients with schizophreniform disorder must demonstrate two of following: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, or disorganized behavior (known as positive symptoms), or negative symptoms (eg, flat affect, apathy, alogia). To meet diagnostic criteria, patients must demonstrate symptoms for greater than 1 month and less than 6 months. Two-thirds of patients with schizophreniform disorder ultimately develop schizophrenia. Cognitive impairment is commonly one of the early signs of schizophrenia. Schizophrenia has been postulated to result from excessive pruning of glutamatergic synapses in the cerebral cortex during development, explaining the negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia. Patients commonly experience deficits across several cognitive domains including attention, working memory, verbal learning and memory, and executive function. However, basic cognitive functions such as orientation commonly remain intact. Antipsychotic medications address positive symptoms but do not significantly improve negative or cognitive symptoms. Cognitive training may assist with cognitive deficits.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Abnormal amyloid precursor protein (Choice A) and hyperphosphorylation of the Tau protein (Choice E) are pathologic findings in dementia, Alzheimer type, not schizophrenia. Amyloid plaques are extracellular protein accumulations while tau forms intracytoplasmic and extracellular protein tangles. Adolescent patients are too young to develop dementia, Alzheimer type. Decreased auditory acuity (Choice C) and decreased visual fields (Choice D) are atypical of schizophrenia. Patients with schizophrenia typically experience deficits in higher-order functions mediated by the frontal lobes such as cognition and motivation (eg, cognitive and negative symptoms).

questionStem: Three weeks after voluntarily enter ing a residential treatment facility for alcoholism, a 27-year-o ld woman is being prepared for discharge. She requests medication to control her urge to drink alcohol and decrease her risk for relapse. Prior to admission, she drank 6 to 12 glasses of wine nightly. She tried to quit drinking several times but says her urges to drink returned after 2 to 3 days of abstinence. She has no other history of serious illness and takes no medications. Physical and mental status exam inations show no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Alcohol use disorder refers to an addiction to alcohol that must meet at least two criteria, including an inability to cut back on drinking, drinking more than expected, excessive time spent drinking, alcoho l cravings, persistent drinking despite physical or mental problems related to drinking, and persistent drinking despite negative socia l consequences. Patients with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder may benefit from daily medication. Commonly utilized medications for alcohol use disorder include naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram, and gabapentin. Naltrexone, a long-acting opioid receptor antagonist, blocks the rewarding effects of drinking alcoho l and thinking about alcohol, thereby preventing alcohol cravings.

It is useful in nicotine use disorder but not alcohol use disorder. As a result of its lowering of the seizure threshold, bupropion increases the risk for alcohol withdrawal seizures. Levomethadyl acetate (Choice C) is an opioid receptor agonist similar to methadone. It is utilized as an opioid replacement therapy in refractory opioid use disorder but would not be helpful in alcoho l use disorder. Naloxone (Choice D) is a short-acting opioid receptor antagonist. Its maximum duration of action is approximately 2 hours, which would necessitate multiple doses daily to prevent alcohol cravings. questionStem: As a condition of employment, a newly hired police officer has agreed to avoid the use of all illicit drugs bo th on and off duty and to provide random urine samp les for drug screening. Although he has not used any drugs in the past month, his urine samp le shows a definite positive reaction. Which of the following drugs would most likely account for this finding?
correctExplanation: The psychoactive component of cannabis is f1-9 tetrahydrocannabino l (THC). THC is lipophilic and therefore distributes widely across body tissues (eg, adipose tissue, heart, lungs, and liver). As a resu lt of its wide distribution and slow release from body stores, THC has a long half-life and may lead to positive urine toxico logy screening up to 50 days after the last use. Patients who regularly use cannabis are more likely to demonstrate persistent ly positive urine drug screenings.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Cocaine (Choice A), heroin (Choice B), LSD (Choice C), and methamphetamine (Choice E) are not as widely distributed as cannabis and possess shorter half-lives. Urine drug screens are typically negative a few days after the patient's last use. Educationa l Objective: Compared with other recreational drugs, cannabis has a long half-life. In chronic users, urine toxicology screenings may remain positive up to 50 days after the patient 's last use.

questionStem: A 19-yea r-old man is brought to the physician by his parents because of changes in his behavior during the past 6 months. During this time, he has been obsessed with what he calls "the ultima te truth of the universe" and has spent most of his time in his room alone. His parents say that he has always been serious, curious, and quiet. The few friends he had stopped interacting with him because of this behavio r. The patient explains that he needs to solve "the ultimate and consummate algorithmic result." He has no history of serious illness . He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 98 kg (217 lb); BMI is 33 kg/m 2. His pulse is 82/min, and blood pressure is 116/77 mm Hg. Physical examination shows abdominal striae. On menta l status examination, he describes his mood as "transfixed. " He has a blunt affect. His thoug ht process is disorganized, and he continues to talk about the equation. There is no evidence of suicidal ideatio n. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. Urine toxicology screening is negative . A CT scan of the head shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: According to the DSM-5, patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders demonstrate at least two of the following five symptoms: delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, or negative symptoms (eg, flat or blunted affect, apathy, alogia). Delusions, hallucinations, and disorganization are referred to as positive symptoms. To meet the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia, patients must demonstrate functional deficits, and the total duration of symptoms must exceed 6 months. This patient demonstrates delusional thinking (a fixed belief that he needs to solve a problem of the universe), disorganized thinking orspeech, and negative symptoms (isolating to his room, a blunted affect). Many patients with schizophrenia are social ly anxious prior to the onset of psychotic symptoms. Management requires antipsychotic medication (eg, ziprasidone, an atypical antipsychotic). Antipsychotic medications antagonize the dopamine receptor, addressing excessive dopaminergic signaling in the mesolimbic pathway (postu lated to underlie positive psychotic symptoms), though they do not address the negative or cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Buspirone (Choice A) is a serotonin modulator utilized to treat genera lized anxiety disorder. Clonazepam (Choice B) is a benzodiazepine medication utilized to treat acute episodes of anxiety. Neither would address psychotic symptoms.

questionStem: A 42-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examinat ion for insurance purposes. When asked for an emergency contact, he gives the name of his mother but says that she lives in another state and that he has not seen her for 5 years. He lives by himself and says that he has no friends. He spends most of his free time alone in his apartment cutting out articles about animals from magazines and newspapers that he plans to use in the future. He has worked the graveyard shift of his company for 10 years with few absences. On two occasions, he was offered a day shift but refused. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. He is wearing mismatched socks, and his glasses are tied to a piece of twine he wears around his neck. Physical examinat ion shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. His thoughts are goal directed but difficult to understand because of his frequent use of idiosyncratic metaphors. He reports no auditory or visual hallucinations. He can recall three of three objects after 5 minutes and describes events of the past several years without difficulty. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Schizotypal personality disorder is a cluster A personality disorder, the odd or eccentric cluster. The disorder is characterized by odd behavior and thinking and a constricted affect. Patients with schizotypa l personality disorder may have strange, overly metaphorical or magical thinking, though they fluctuate in the degree of their conviction about these beliefs (which differentiates these beliefs from the fixed delusions of schizophrenia). The strange beliefs may also manifest as eccentric appearance as in this patient. Patients may experience somatosensory illusions or other abnormal perceptions. Patients with schizotypal personality disorder may appear to lack interest in cultivating relationships (eg, work graveyard shifts) and, because of an inability to interpret others' motivations, may be deeply distrustful and anxious around others. Personality disorders are persistently maladaptive ways of relating to the self and to society that typically appear by early adulthood.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Agoraphobia (Choice A) refers to the fear of leaving one's home. Though this patient lacks an interest in socializing, he leaves his home to work the graveyard shift. . - - -- - - - - -- -- - ~ - ~ -- -- - - -- - - - ·

He attributes his symptoms to the stress related to his 21-year-old daughter's weddi ng plans. He divorced his wife 11 years ago because he felt more sexually attracted to men than women. This patient is experiencing distress and anxiety symptoms related to the possibi lity of difficulties with his daughter 's fiance 's parents at his daughter 's wedding because of his sexual orientation. As adjustment disorder is typical ly self-limited, the treatment of adjustment disorder commonly includes brief supportive psychotherapy.

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman with major depressive disorder is brought to the physician by her daughter for a follow-up examination. During the past 6 months, she has received trials of citalopram, fluvoxam ine, and escitalopram with no improvement in her symptoms. Four weeks ago, she was switched from fluoxetine to sertraline therapy because the fluoxetine caused excessive tiredness . Her daughter reports that the patient is "slightly better, but not dramat ically so." She has had a decreased appetite resulting in a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss during the past 3 months. Today, her eyes are closed throughout most of the visit. She appears cachectic and disheve led. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 43 kg (95 lb); BMI is 16 kg/m2. Physical examinat ion shows poor skin turgor and severe psychomotor retardat ion. On menta l status exam ination, she respo nds to few of the physician's questions and uses only brief responses . There is no evidence of suicida l ideation or psychot ic symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Add buprop ion to her current medicat ion regimen
choices.B: Add olanzapine to her current medication regimen
choices.C: Switch from sertraline to nortripty line
