correctExplanation: Symptoms of major depressive disorder (MOD) include two or more weeks of at least five of the following symptoms: depressed mood, anhedonia (eg, decreased interest in socia lizing), guilt or worth lessness, difficu lty concentrating, suicidal thoughts, or neurovegetative symptoms (decreased energy, sleep disturbance, appetite disturbance). These symptoms disrupt everyday functioning. This patient's functional impairment is so severe that she is minimal ly interactive and appears disheveled. Her neurovegetative symptoms have led to physical deterioration, including significant weight loss and nutritiona l compromise. The patient requires admission to the psychiatric unit to prevent further physica l deterioration and so she can receive an inpatient course of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). ECT utilizes electrical current to induce a generalized seizure under general anesthesia, which is postulated to increase monoamine activity and promote neurogenesis. Indications include depression that is refractory to multiple medication classes and depression associated with catatonia, nutritional compromise and dehydration, psychotic features, or persistent suicida l intent. Depression may begin to improve immediately after the first ECT session, whereas antidepressant medication takes weeks to work. Further, ECT has an increased effectiveness compared with antidepressant medications. Adverse events common ly include transient memory loss and the risks of general anesthesia (eg, cardiovascu lar events, postoperative confusion).
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Adding bupropion or olanzapine to an antidepressant regimen (Choices A and B) are augmentation strategies utilized in patients with a significant partial response to the initial antidepressant. This patient minimal ly responded to sertraline. Further, these augmentation strategies typically take weeks to be effective, whereas this patient is nutritiona lly compromised and requires rapid treatment.

questionStem: A 25-year-o ld man is admitted to the hospital because of extreme hyperactiv ity for 2 days. He is unable to conduct an intelligent conversation because of flight of ideas. He is started on haloperidol therapy (10 mg daily). Two days later, he has difficulty breathing, uncontrollable tightening of his face and neck muscles with spasm, and a rolling up and locking of his eyes. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: Acute dystonic reactions are involuntary, painful muscle spasms that occur most frequent ly in response to potent dopamine-2 (D2) antagonists such as typical antipsychotics (eg, haloperidol). Common presentations include torticollis (head tilted to the side and down), retrocollis (head tilted back), opisthotonos (arching of the back), and oculogyric crisis (upward deviation of the eyes). Patients rarely present with laryngospasm and strider. The underlying pathophysio logy is an imbalance in the dopaminergic-cholinergic pathways of the basal ganglia. Risk factors for development include male sex, young age, recent cocaine use, and a history of previous acute dystonic reaction. Acute dystonic reactions are treated with diphenhydramine or benztropine, which are both anticholinergic medications that work to restore the proper balance in the dopaminergic and cholinergic pathways.

It does not act on skeletal muscle and would therefore be unhelpful in acute dystonic reactions. Chlordiazepoxide (Choice B) is a benzodiazepine medication most commonly utilized for alcohol withdrawal. Clonazepam (Choice C) is a benzodiazepine medication commonly utilized to treat anxiety and rapid-eye movement sleep behavior disorder. Benzodiazepines such as lorazepam may also be utilized to treat antipsychotic-induced akathisia. However, these medications do not restore the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia and are therefore ineffective for an acute dystonic reaction. However, propranolol does not restore the dopamine-acetylcholine balance in the basal ganglia and is therefore ineffective for an acute dystonic reaction. Two years ago, he completed a 5-year prison sentence for assault. He was treated in a psychiatric hospital for conduct disorder at the age of 15 years. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He has a history of drinking excessive amounts of alcohol and using illicit drugs. He is cooperative with the hospita l staff but becomes irritable when the police officer who is guarding him attempts to interact with him. His tempera ture is 36.6°C (97.8°F), pulse is 78/min, and blood pressure is 132/82 mm Hg. Physical examination shows no abnormalities except for multiple scars over the face. On questioning, he says that he got the scars in fights. On mental status examination, there is no evidence of depression or psychosis. questionStem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after s he became agitated and disruptive on an airplane. She was screaming and using profanity, and the plane was forced to land. On arrival, she is agitated and hypervig ilant, and her speech is rapid and pressured. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. Examination shows warm dry skin. The pupils are 8 mm bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Acetylcholine activity in the brain mediates attention and motivation, and periphera l acetylcho line mediates smooth muscle contraction. Diphenhydramine, an antihistamine medication with strong anticho linergic activity, is commonly utilized off-label for acute episodes of anxiety (eg, secondary to flying). Anticholinergic agents commonly cause delirium (as evidenced by this patient's agitated behavior) along with smooth muscle dysfunction (decreased function of sweat glands and pupillary muscles leading to this patient's flushed skin and mydriasis, respectively). Anticho linergic toxicity typically manifests as delirium, sedation, hallucinations, ataxia, mydriasis, visual disturbances (cycloplegia, or loss of accommodation), dry mouth, tachycardia, urinary retention, constipation, and flushed skin. Management includes discontinuation of the offending agent, supportive care with gentle sedation, fluids, and prevention of hyperthermia, seizure, or arrhythmias. In severe cases, treatment with pyridostigmine, a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, may be initiated.

Treatment may include hospitalization and antipsychotic treatment depending on symptom severity and functional impairment, though some symptoms or the entire presentation may resolve without medications.

questionStem: A 19-year-old college sophomore comes to the physician because of episodes of shortness of breath, palpitations, and sweating that have awakened him from sleep several times over the past 2 months. He says that the episodes are so alarming that he thinks he is going to die and is afraid that he has a serious illness. He reports episodes of sadness since he broke up with his girlfriend 3 weeks ago. He does not smoke, drink alcohol, or use illicit drugs. He requests a bronchodilator inhaler. His pulse is 80/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Panic attacks feature acute fear or anxiety that peaks within minutes and is associated with four additional physical symptoms or associated mental states. These additional symptoms may include heart palpitations or tachycardia, shortness of breath, chest pain, dizziness, the sensation of choking, gastrointestinal distress, paresthesias, sweating, chills, trembling, derealization, the fear of dying, or the fear of losing control. These episodes may occur during calm or anxious states, in the daytime or nighttime. The pathogenesis involves genetic factors, an anxious temperament, and stressful life events. In patients with an initial episode of panic symptoms, a thorough history and physical examination along with a basic laboratory workup and a potential ECG should be performed. Panic disorder is a relatively common psychiatric disorder characterized by recurrent panic attacks that are unexpected and associated with worry about future panic attacks or avoidance of panic attack triggers. Treatment of panic disorder typically includes antidepressant medication and/or cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) with a focus on graded exposure to the feared situation.
